table.title: UAX #14 Table 1. Line Breaking Classes (excerpt)
table.html:
ClassDescriptive NameExamplesBehavior
Non-tailorable Line Breaking Classes
BKMandatory BreakNL, PARAGRAPH SEPARATORCause a line break (after)
CRCarriage ReturnCRCause a line break (after), except between CR and LF
LFLine FeedLFCause a line break (after)
CMCombining MarkCombining marks, control codesProhibit a line break between the character and the preceding character
NLNext LineNELCause a line break (after)
SGSurrogateSurrogatesDo not occur in well-formed text
WJWord JoinerWJProhibit line breaks before and after
ZWZero Width SpaceZWSPProvide a break opportunity
GLNon-breaking (“Glue”)CGJ, NBSP, ZWNBSPProhibit line breaks before and after
SPSpaceSPACEEnable indirect line breaks
ZWJZero Width JoinerZero Width JoinerProhibit line breaks within joiner sequences
Break Opportunities
B2Break Opportunity Before and AfterEm dashProvide a line break opportunity before and after the character
BABreak AfterSpaces, most sentence-terminal punctuationGenerally provide a line break opportunity after the character
BBBreak BeforePunctuation used in dictionariesGenerally provide a line break opportunity before the character
table.edits: first two groups (14 classes); italics removed

d1.purpose: Identify Unicode line breaking classes and explain their names, representative characters, and behavior.
tasks: Look up a class code and read across to its name, examples, and behavior.
Compare the behavior of related classes, especially where breaking is permitted or prohibited.
Read sequentially through the two groups to understand the range of classes.
relations: Each class code identifies one row; the name expands the code, examples illustrate it, and behavior states its effect on line breaking.
The full-width group labels divide non-tailorable classes from break-opportunity classes.
Before, after, and between distinctions in behavior are essential to comparison.
roles: Class is a compact row header and lookup key.
Descriptive Name connects the code to a recognizable concept.
Examples identify characters or categories associated with the class.
Behavior carries the main explanatory and comparison text.
keep_whole: Class codes and short character identifiers such as ZWJ, ZWSP, and ZWNBSP.
Individual words where space permits, especially technical terms and directional qualifiers.
may_wrap: Example lists at spaces or punctuation.
Behavior statements between words, while keeping their reading order clear.
Group labels and column headings at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: Rows within each group should support consistent scanning, even when longer entries require extra lines.
The two full-width group labels share the same structural role.
Examples and descriptive names both support identification, but behavior deserves more room for its longer explanations.
d1.h_vs_v: A viewport-fitting table keeps each row visible across the screen but forces narrow text columns, long rows, and some split words. A wider table preserves words and reduces vertical fragmentation, at the cost of horizontal scrolling and losing some columns from the initial view.

d2.purpose: A reference for identifying Unicode line-breaking classes and understanding their behavior.
tasks: Find a class by its abbreviation or descriptive name.
Connect a class to representative characters and its line-breaking behavior.
Compare related behaviors across classes within each section.
relations: Each row connects one class abbreviation to its name, examples, and behavior.
The merged section rows group classes by their role in line breaking.
The behavior column carries the main distinctions readers need to compare.
roles: Class is the compact row identifier and lookup key.
Descriptive Name expands the class abbreviation.
Examples ground the class in characters or character types.
Behavior explains the effect on line breaking.
Merged rows are section headings, not class entries.
keep_whole: Class abbreviations and character identifiers such as ZWJ, ZWSP, and ZWNBSP.
Individual words where space permits, especially technical terms and hyphenated examples.
Relationships such as before and after, and the exception between CR and LF.
may_wrap: Example lists at commas or between words.
Behavior descriptions at natural phrase boundaries.
same_scale: The name and example columns serve related identification tasks, though their content lengths differ.
All behavior cells should have the same width so their statements can be scanned consistently.
d2.h_vs_v: A viewport-fitting table keeps each row visible at once but forces long words to split and makes rows tall. A wider table preserves words and reduces height, at the cost of scrolling between identifiers and behavior; extra width is most useful in the explanatory columns.

d3.purpose: Provide a reference for identifying Unicode line breaking classes and understanding their behavior.
tasks: Find a class by its short code or descriptive name.
Read across a row to connect the class with examples and its line breaking behavior.
Compare behaviors and examples across related classes.
Locate classes within the two named groups.
relations: Each row associates one class code with its name, examples and behavior.
The full-width group headings classify the rows that follow them.
Behavior descriptions distinguish closely related classes, including before and after break opportunities.
roles: Class codes are compact row labels and lookup keys.
Descriptive names identify the meaning of each code.
Examples show representative characters, character names or categories.
Column headers identify attributes; merged headings organize groups of rows.
keep_whole: Class codes and character identifiers such as ZWJ, ZWSP, NBSP and ZWNBSP.
Individual words and meaningful terms such as sentence-terminal where space permits.
The distinction between before and after in behavior descriptions.
may_wrap: Example lists at commas or between words.
Behavior descriptions at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: Class codes need a consistently compact column.
Descriptive names and examples both need enough room for multiword entries, though their widths need not match.
Behavior merits more space than the other prose columns because its rules are generally longer.
d3.h_vs_v: A viewport-fitting table keeps all four attributes visible together but forces some words and identifiers to split and makes rows tall. Scrolling allows intact units and more natural prose, at the cost of moving horizontally between row labels and behavior.

analysis.strengths: The most relaxed full-table setting: no measured word splits, single-line headers, and mostly short, natural lines. The generous Behavior column makes the rules easy to read and compare.
analysis.faults: It requires the greatest horizontal travel. The initial viewport shows essentially none of Behavior, so the table’s principal explanatory information is hidden until the reader scrolls.
analysis.spatial_logic: It gives compact codes their minimum useful width, moderate space to names and examples, and nearly half the table to the longest prose.

analysis.strengths: All four columns are visible at once. Among the fitting layouts it is shorter, and its slightly wider Behavior column helps some long rules.
analysis.faults: It splits nine measured words, including the Descriptive Name header and ordinary names, as well as long example terms. Tall, narrow cells disrupt row scanning and produce large empty areas beside wrapped prose.
analysis.spatial_logic: It divides the remaining width fairly evenly after reserving space for Class, favoring Behavior slightly at the expense of names.

analysis.strengths: The whole table is visible without horizontal scrolling. Extra name width keeps Mandatory and Combining intact compared with Q.
analysis.faults: The header and several example terms still split inside words. The narrower Behavior column makes the Combining Mark rule eight lines tall, increasing height and weakening row-to-row comparison.
analysis.spatial_logic: It transfers four pixels from Behavior to Descriptive Name while keeping Examples unchanged, trading some prose flow for better name breaks.

analysis.strengths: It fits the viewport and has the fewest measured word splits of the fitting candidates. The extra pixel in Examples lets dictionaries remain whole and improves the GL example grouping.
analysis.faults: Six measured word splits remain, including in the header and important example terms. Behavior is still extremely narrow, and the table is as tall as R.
analysis.spatial_logic: It makes a one-pixel adjustment to R in favor of Examples, exploiting a useful wrapping threshold without changing the overall four-column compression.

analysis.strengths: It keeps words intact, all headers on one line, and cells to at most three lines while requiring substantially less scrolling than P. Its first three columns make class lookup and example scanning comfortable.
analysis.faults: Behavior begins at the edge of the initial viewport and is effectively hidden. Its narrower prose column increases row heights and creates some spare space in the other columns.
analysis.spatial_logic: It retains P’s roomy identification columns but reduces Examples slightly and cuts Behavior substantially, balancing horizontal travel against vertical expansion.

analysis.strengths: It has the least horizontal travel of the scrolling candidates and no measured word splits. The first viewport includes all three identification columns and a visible start of Behavior.
analysis.faults: The Behavior text is cut off at the initial viewport edge, requiring scrolling to read it. The name header wraps, and several names and examples become noticeably taller, especially in the final section.
analysis.spatial_logic: It compresses all three text columns relative to T, accepting more wrapping in exchange for a narrower table.

rounds.insights: The fitting layouts make all columns immediately available, but their width budget cannot accommodate the measured longest units in all three text columns: even their minimum widths total 376 px with Class and padding. Some within-word breaks are therefore unavoidable. Small width changes can nevertheless move breaks across useful thresholds. Scrolling preserves words and improves the reading of rules, but the first viewport must be judged separately: P and T conceal Behavior, while U only hints at it. Row height also matters because a long rule creates blank space across the other columns.

analysis.strengths: All words remain intact, and the class codes, names and examples are visible together on initial view. Behavior has enough room for mostly natural phrases.
analysis.faults: The descriptive header wraps, and the BA example occupies four lines. Only a sliver of Behavior appears initially, so its values require scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: The narrow code column is appropriate; the remaining width favors Behavior. Several rows are nevertheless made tall by the narrower name and example columns.

analysis.strengths: It is the narrowest scrolling option and preserves whole words. The initial view includes the class codes, names and examples, with a small glimpse of Behavior.
analysis.faults: The narrower name column splits common names and stretches B2 to four lines. The narrower Behavior column adds wrapping, while the 30 px width saving over s0B does little to change the initial view.
analysis.spatial_logic: Its width reduction comes at the cost of a taller, more fragmented table, especially near the bottom.

analysis.strengths: All four columns are visible at once, making it possible to associate a class with its behavior without horizontal scrolling.
analysis.faults: The header, identifiers and ordinary words split within words, including PARAGRAPH, SEPARATOR and punctuation. Long, narrow blocks make comparison difficult and produce a very tall table.
analysis.spatial_logic: The fixed code column leaves too little space for the other three columns. Equal-looking narrow text columns cannot accommodate their different content demands.

analysis.strengths: All headers fit on one line, words stay intact, and names and examples wrap naturally. The full table has a compact, steady rhythm, with no cell exceeding three lines.
analysis.faults: Behavior is entirely outside the initial viewport, making its existence less apparent and requiring scrolling for a central reading task. Its long entries still wrap across several lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first three columns fill the viewport almost exactly, providing a clear lookup view while placing Behavior in a separate horizontal reading area.

rounds.insights: T is the strongest scrolling layout: modest increases in name and example width improve several rows at once. Its initial viewport, however, hides the Behavior column completely. S demonstrates the cost of fitting everything at once; a better fit would reserve enough width for the longest units in the name and example columns, accepting narrower Behavior text. Both classes deserve separate consideration.

analysis.strengths: All headers fit on one line, words remain intact, and the first viewport shows class codes, names and examples.
analysis.faults: Behavior is almost entirely outside the initial viewport. The narrow Examples column gives BK three lines and BA four, while several Behavior cells also leave short final lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: The compact total width reduces scrolling, but the savings in Examples and Behavior produce taller, less even rows.

analysis.strengths: Natural word breaks, single-line headers and a three-line maximum make this the clearest scrolling layout. The wider Examples column keeps Zero Width Joiner together and reduces wrapping in BK and BB; the wider Behavior column shortens several rows.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport shows no Behavior column, so interpreting a class requires horizontal scrolling. At the far right, the class codes will be outside the viewport. Some Behavior lines still end with isolated words.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first three columns occupy essentially the full viewport, creating a clean lookup view; the additional width is concentrated in the prose column, where it substantially reduces height.

analysis.strengths: The first viewport has the same useful class, name and example view as s1C. Headers and words remain intact, and no cell exceeds three lines.
analysis.faults: Behavior remains outside the initial viewport. Its narrower width creates extra lines in SG and the break-opportunity rows, including short final lines, making the table taller than s1C.
analysis.spatial_logic: It preserves s1C's first-screen lookup area while saving 20 px of horizontal travel, but the saving costs considerable vertical space.

analysis.strengths: All four columns are visible together without horizontal scrolling, so class codes can be compared directly with behavior.
analysis.faults: The Descriptive Name header and words such as PARAGRAPH, SEPARATOR, Opportunity and punctuation split within words. Behavior becomes a narrow stack of up to eight lines, making lookup and comparison slow; the tall rows leave large blank areas in shorter cells.
analysis.spatial_logic: Nearly equal allocations to the three content columns give too little room to both long identifiers and prose. The resulting height and irregular density are the price of showing the full grid at once.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve words and make the table much easier to read, but their first viewport hides the Behavior information central to interpreting each class. Increasing Examples from 130 to 150 px and Behavior from 230 to 250 px improves lineation and reduces height substantially. The fitted layout keeps every column in view but cannot accommodate all measured unbreakable units at once; its widths should therefore be tested as a deliberate tradeoff between word integrity and usable prose.

analysis.strengths: All words remain intact, headers fit on one line, and the relatively wide Behavior column keeps explanations compact. The first viewport shows the class, name, and examples together.
analysis.faults: The entire Behavior column starts beyond the initial viewport, so understanding what a class does requires scrolling. The table extends 272px beyond the viewport.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first three columns occupy the initial screen almost exactly; the fourth forms a readable but separate field to the right. Shorter rows make cross-row scanning easier than in s1C.

analysis.strengths: All four columns are visible together, making it possible to associate classes with their behavior without horizontal scrolling.
analysis.faults: Seven internal word breaks disrupt reading, including the header, Mandatory, Combining, PARAGRAPH, and SEPARATOR. Narrow Behavior lines make the table very tall and leave large empty areas alongside long cells.
analysis.spatial_logic: Nearly equal allocations to the three content columns preserve the whole grid on screen but provide too little text width for their different contents.

analysis.strengths: Words and headers remain intact, and the first viewport presents complete class, name, and example columns. It requires 20px less horizontal travel than s2A.
analysis.faults: Behavior remains entirely offscreen initially. Its narrower width adds lines and height, including a short final line in the WJ and GL behavior cells.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first three columns match s2A; reducing Behavior saves horizontal space but produces a slightly less compact vertical rhythm.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible at once, and the small increase in name width keeps Mandatory and Combining intact. It has one fewer measured internal word break than s2C.
analysis.faults: The name header and several important terms still split inside words; the narrower Examples column also splits punctuation in the BA row. Behavior remains fragmented into short lines, and the table is as tall as s2C.
analysis.spatial_logic: Two pixels move from Examples to Descriptive Name, improving some name entries at the expense of example text without changing the overall height.

rounds.insights: The scrolling layouts preserve words and make the table substantially easier to scan, but their initial view hides the behavior that gives each class meaning. The fitting layouts expose every field while forcing word breaks and long, uneven rows. A useful refinement is to test a narrower first-screen grouping that reveals at least the start of Behavior, and to redistribute the fitting layout toward the longest unbreakable words.

bad.why: The narrow descriptive-name column splits ordinary words such as “Mandatory” and “Combining”; examples also break inside words.
The examples column breaks several words, including “Surrogates” and “dictionaries,” making lookup and continuous reading difficult.
The shorter table comes at the cost of nine internal word breaks, including breaks in class names and examples.
It splits the descriptive header and several example words, with more internal word breaks than Layout S.

contrast.why: Equal-looking columns waste space on short class codes while forcing names, examples and behavior into narrow, fragmented lines.

synthesis.rationale: s2A keeps words whole, gives behavior enough width for readable phrases, and keeps the first three columns visible together at the initial scroll position. Layout S is the strongest fitting candidate because it has the fewest measured internal word breaks, although its split header and examples remain serious compromises. The scrolling alternatives are publishable, but P requires more horizontal travel, T wraps behavior more often, and s3A wraps names and examples more heavily.

general: Size columns for their content and reading roles, preserving meaningful words and identifiers where possible.
Judge a scrolling table both as a complete grid and at its initial viewport position.
Consider row height and horizontal travel together with readability; neither compactness nor equal widths is an end in itself.
specific: The class codes need little width, while behavior needs substantially more space for prose.
Keeping class, descriptive name and examples together in the initial viewport supports lookup before scrolling to behavior.
At the fixed 360px width, the provided fitting candidates all split words; Layout S is a constrained finalist, not an uncompromised solution.

synthesis.tradeoffs: s2A requires 272px of horizontal scrolling, and behavior is initially offscreen. Layout S exposes all columns at once but produces an 1850px table, very narrow prose and six measured breaks inside words. P improves wrapping and table height at the cost of 332px of scrolling.
synthesis.uncertain: The fitting selection is the best of the rendered fitting candidates, not a claim that no other width allocation could improve it. Acceptance depends on whether avoiding horizontal scrolling outweighs Layout S’s visible word fragmentation for this publication.

critique.good: All four columns are visible together, so each class can be read across without scrolling. The group labels remain clear.
critique.problems: Words break awkwardly in the heading and body, including Mandatory, PARAGRAPH, SEPARATOR and punctuation. Long, uneven rows make related behaviors difficult to compare.
critique.cause: The 92px name and 100px examples columns are narrower than some words plus padding. The 106px behavior column fragments explanations into many short lines.

critique.good: Words remain whole and the columns have a useful hierarchy. Most names and examples are easy to scan, and the full render keeps explanations reasonably compact.
critique.problems: Behavior is entirely outside the initial viewport, and the right edge cuts through some examples. Several behavior statements wrap just before directional qualifiers, slowing comparison.
critique.cause: The first three columns total 371px, placing behavior beyond the 360px viewport. At 260px, behavior is readable but still wraps several key phrases.

critique.good: The generous behavior width keeps many explanations on one or two lines, and the long B2 name fits on one line. Words remain whole.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows little more than class and name, with examples cut off and behavior hidden. The broad name column leaves considerable empty space in most rows and increases the scroll distance.
critique.cause: The 263px name column is sized for one exceptional entry. Together with the 180px examples and 320px behavior columns, it makes the table 825px wide.

critique.good: All four columns are visible at once, class codes are easy to locate, and the group labels remain clear.
critique.problems: Behavior is fragmented into very short lines, with words such as “character” and “opportunity” split. Tall rows and large empty areas in the other columns make reading and comparison laborious.
critique.cause: The 84px Behavior column leaves too little text width; 104px and 110px for the supporting columns take space from the main explanatory column.

critique.good: Words remain intact, Behavior reads in relatively natural phrases, and the full table has a compact, consistent rhythm.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows almost none of Behavior, so the main comparison requires scrolling. The name heading wraps, and some names and examples occupy three lines.
critique.cause: The first three columns total 346px, placing Behavior at the viewport edge. The 135px name column wraps its heading, while the 300px Behavior column contributes substantially to the scroll distance.

critique.good: All columns are visible, and the wider Behavior column makes its statements substantially easier to read than in d1r1A. The table is also shorter.
critique.problems: The heading and several names and examples break inside words, including “Mandatory,” “PARAGRAPH,” and “punctuation.” Long rows still interrupt scanning.
critique.cause: The 92px name and 100px example columns are narrower than some of their words plus padding. The 106px Behavior column remains narrow for sentence-level reading.

critique.good: All headings fit on one line, words remain intact, and names, examples, and behavior have a balanced, compact full-table rhythm.
critique.problems: Behavior is entirely beyond the initial viewport, and the viewport cuts through the last example column. Some behavior statements wrap after directional words, making comparison less immediate.
critique.cause: The first three columns total 371px, exceeding the viewport before Behavior begins. The 260px Behavior column produces some less helpful phrase breaks.

critique.good: All words remain intact, the class codes scan clearly, and the generous behavior column keeps most explanations to one or two lines. Both group labels are clear.
critique.problems: The name heading wraps, and several names and examples form tall, uneven blocks, especially in the final group. The initial viewport shows almost none of the behavior column, so the main comparison requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 140px name and example columns constrain longer entries; together with the 61px class column, they place the behavior column at the viewport edge. The 280px behavior column contributes to the scrolling distance.

critique.good: Every column is visible at once, preserving the connection between each class and its behavior. The codes and group labels remain easy to locate.
critique.problems: Several words split across lines, including the name heading, Mandatory, Combining, punctuation, and dictionaries. Long, narrow behavior blocks make directional comparisons laborious, and the resulting tall rows disrupt scanning.
critique.cause: The 92px name and 100px example columns are narrower than some unbreakable words plus padding. The 106px behavior column also forces frequent wrapping; the 360px total leaves little room to remedy all three.

critique.good: The headings fit on one line, words remain intact, and the wider name and example columns produce a compact, orderly table. The two-line B2 name and most behavior statements read naturally.
critique.problems: The initial viewport hides the entire behavior column and clips the right edge of some examples, so readers must scroll to understand and compare the classes. Some behavior phrases wrap with directional words separated across lines.
critique.cause: The first three columns total 371px, placing behavior beyond the viewport. The 260px behavior width is sufficient for intact words but wraps some longer comparison phrases.

critique.good: The full table is readable and compact, with intact words, clear group labels, and behavior statements that generally wrap naturally. The wider behavior column keeps related prohibitions easy to compare.
critique.problems: The initial viewport shows the lookup code and names but none of the behavior column, and cuts through some example text. Reading across requires substantial scrolling.
critique.cause: The first three columns total 371 px, placing Behavior entirely beyond the 360 px viewport; its 320 px width also makes this the widest design.

critique.good: All words remain intact, and the shorter overall width reduces scrolling. The first viewport shows complete codes and most identification content.
critique.problems: The name header wraps, several short names acquire extra lines, and the B2 name and BA example become particularly tall. Only a sliver of Behavior appears initially, so it is not yet usable without scrolling.
critique.cause: The 130 px name and example columns are too narrow for several common phrases; the 260 px behavior column also creates more wrapping than in d1r3B.

critique.good: All four columns are visible together, preserving the immediate connection between class and behavior. The group labels and codes remain clear.
critique.problems: Words break across lines in the header, names, and examples, including distracting single-letter fragments. Long behavior cells make rows very tall and interrupt comparison down the table.
critique.cause: The 92 px name and 100 px example columns fall below their measured unbreakable content needs; the 106 px behavior column leaves little room for phrases.

critique.good: Codes, names, and examples scan well, words remain intact, and the table is shorter than d1r3C while requiring less scrolling than d1r3B.
critique.problems: Behavior is entirely outside the initial viewport. Its narrower measure produces isolated 'after' lines in the WJ and GL rows and a three-line CM explanation, weakening comparison and adding uneven row height.
critique.cause: The first three columns total 371 px, and the 260 px behavior column is too narrow for several useful phrase groupings.

critique.good: Class codes and text remain whole, and most rows have a comfortable, consistent rhythm. The first viewport shows the class, name and examples together.
critique.problems: The two-line name heading makes the header taller; B2 and BA are noticeably taller than neighboring rows. Behavior is entirely beyond the initial viewport, so the main explanation requires scrolling.
critique.cause: The 145 px name column falls just short of fitting its heading and makes the B2 name three lines; the 150 px examples column makes the BA example three lines. The first three columns occupy 356 px.

critique.good: Words and identifiers remain whole, and the beginning of Behavior is visible initially. The 320 px behavior column reads comfortably in the full table.
critique.problems: Names and examples wrap into narrow stacks, producing uneven, tall rows and slowing comparisons. The initial glimpse of Behavior is too narrow to convey most statements.
critique.cause: The 120 px name and 110 px examples columns force several ordinary phrases across multiple lines. Together with the class column, they leave only 69 px of Behavior in the initial viewport.

critique.good: All headings fit on one line, words remain whole, and the relatively compact rows make the groups easy to scan. Names, examples and behavior have a more balanced rhythm than in the other scrolling renders.
critique.problems: Behavior is completely outside the initial viewport, and the right edge cuts through some examples at first sight. Reading across a row requires substantial horizontal travel.
critique.cause: The 150 px name and 160 px examples columns give the identification fields useful space but put Behavior at 371 px; the 320 px behavior column increases the total scroll distance.

critique.good: All four columns and both group labels are visible across the viewport, keeping each row's fields in view together.
critique.problems: Words split across lines in names and examples, including the heading, and behavior statements become narrow vertical stacks. Very tall rows and large empty areas in shorter cells make lookup and comparison difficult.
critique.cause: The 92 px name and 100 px examples columns are narrower than their longest words plus padding; the 106 px behavior column leaves little room for continuous phrases.

acceptance.unsure: D is the strongest fitting option shown, though its broken words make it a compromised choice. E is the strongest scrolling option overall; C is a close alternative if fewer behavior wraps matter more than scroll distance. The balance depends on how often readers need to compare class codes with behavior on a phone.

ref_equal.why: All columns fit, but words and identifiers fragment repeatedly, including the Examples header and PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR. Tall rows and unused space in the class column make scanning laborious.

d2r0B.why: Words remain intact and the columns have useful proportions. Several behavior descriptions wrap to three lines, and the entire Behavior column lies beyond the initial viewport.

d1r3B.why: Behavior descriptions read fluently and most rows are compact. The wide table demands substantial horizontal scrolling, and the initial view gives no indication of the Behavior column.

s2A.why: Natural breaks and a generous Behavior column make the full table easy to read, with less horizontal travel than C. The initial viewport still excludes Behavior, which is central to the reference task.

d3r4B.why: Words stay whole and the beginning of Behavior is visible, signalling that more content lies to the right. Narrower columns produce frequent wrapping and unevenly tall rows, particularly in the final section.

d3r0A.why: The whole table fits and the class column is sensibly narrow. However, the Descriptive header, PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR and punctuation are split within words, while Behavior often runs down many short lines.

contrast.why: The Examples header fits, but frequent internal word breaks remain throughout the body. Equal columns give short class codes excessive space while long descriptions create very tall, sparse rows.

ref_auto.why: Words stay intact and almost the whole table is initially visible. Behavior is still squeezed into many short lines, and the small horizontal overflow cuts off the ends of some lines until the reader scrolls.

acceptance.unsure: F is the strongest of the fitting layouts, though its broken words make it poor in absolute terms. D is the best balance among the scrolling layouts; C is a close alternative if smoother Behavior text matters more than horizontal travel. H avoids internal word breaks with little overflow, but that overflow is easy to miss.

s2A.why: Headers and class codes stay whole, and the text wraps naturally. The initial viewport shows the first three columns, but Behavior requires scrolling.
